title: US Removes Syria From Terror List, Ending Decades of Isolation as Washington Launches 'Economic Outcast' Campaign on Iran
subhead: Washington formally delisted Syria from its state sponsors of terrorism list, clearing the last major barrier to the country's re-entry into the global financial system, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled a new wave of sanctions targeting Iran's trading partners.

sections.heading: Syria's Long Road Back to the Global Economy
sections.body:
The United States formally removed Syria from its state sponsors of terrorism list on Monday, completing a delisting process that began when President Donald Trump notified Congress on July 8 and passed a 45-day review period over the weekend, according to Al Jazeera. The designation had been in place since 1979, under Hafez al-Assad, and survived the regime's collapse in December 2024.

Analysts told Al Jazeera the removal clears one of the last major hurdles to Syria's integration into the global financial system. Vittorio Maresca di Serracapriola, sanctions lead analyst for Karam Shaar Advisory, called it 'the last main barrier to banks reconnecting with the global community.' Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said the country has 'shaken off' its past, and the delisting follows the earlier removal of sanctions on al-Sharaa and his Hayat Tahrir al-Sham movement. The economy remains weak, with nearly 90 percent of the population living below the poverty line, but the move is expected to ease financing and export restrictions that had deterred banks and investors.
sections.whyItMatters: The delisting is a landmark in the post-Assad reordering of the Middle East: it signals Washington's willingness to reintegrate a former pariah state into the international system, and it gives the new Damascus government a path to reconstruction financing at a moment when the region is otherwise consumed by the Iran war.

sections.heading: Washington's 'Economic Outcast' Campaign Targets Iran's Trading Partners
sections.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced a new round of sanctions on nearly 60 individuals and entities, describing the campaign as the 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran, according to Al Jazeera. 'Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,' Bessent said. The measures target networks accused of helping Iran generate oil revenue, procure weapons and conduct cyberoperations, spanning the Middle East, China, Singapore, Hong Kong and Europe.

The push drew immediate pushback. China said it will safeguard its own interests, insisting sanctions will not resolve the conflict, while Qatar's Foreign Ministry called the measures unilateral, Al Jazeera reported. Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh rejected the sanctions, saying Tehran has programs to counter them. The campaign focuses on five sectors Washington says sustain Iran's economy: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
sections.whyItMatters: The sanctions mark an escalation from targeting Iran itself to pressuring every country that trades with it, a move that risks straining Washington's relations with China and Gulf states even as it seeks to isolate Tehran economically during a war now in its sixth month.

sections.heading: Pakistan's Army Chief Reports 'Significant Progress' in Tehran
sections.body:
Pakistan's Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi completed a daylong diplomatic mission to Tehran on Monday, and Pakistani officials said 'significant progress' was made in talks aimed at ending the US-Israel war on Iran, according to Al Jazeera. It was Munir's third visit to Iran this year. He met President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei.

The Pakistani military said discussions focused on preventing further escalation, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and expediting the conflict's end, and on restoring the Islamabad MoU, the interim ceasefire framework that expired last week. Naqvi said the meeting 'concluded on a highly positive note.' Iran's Tasnim news agency quoted Pezeshkian as telling Munir the US 'must correct its tone and approach' and that American 'intimidation' would complicate implementing the MoU. The diplomatic push comes as Washington warns of severe penalties for any country supporting Iran and Tehran threatens to shut down Gulf oil exports.
sections.whyItMatters: Pakistan has become the indispensable intermediary in a war with no direct US-Iran channel, and its claim of progress offers the clearest sign yet that a diplomatic track, however fragile, remains alive alongside the economic and military confrontation.

sections.heading: UK Shares Missile Blueprints With Ukraine as Russia Warns of Attacks on British Factories
sections.body:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham made Kyiv his first foreign trip on Monday, where Britain agreed to declassify blueprints for British-made components of the Scalp missile, a French-produced version of the Storm Shadow with a range of about 240km, according to Al Jazeera. The move lets Ukraine manufacture the long-range missiles domestically.

Moscow reacted sharply. Kremlin adviser Andrei Fedorov told the BBC he could not 'exclude 100 percent' that there might be 'semi-military' action against Britain, suggesting drone factories producing for Ukraine could come under attack from 'unknown sources.' Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the UK is 'participating in this war' and adding 'fuel to the fire.' Burnham responded in Kyiv by asking reporters who started the fire in the first place. The escalation comes as Russia prepares for a winter offensive and reports grow of coercive recruitment tactics inside Russia, with Al Jazeera documenting alleged press-ganging in Penza and other cities.
sections.whyItMatters: By transferring missile production know-how, the UK is moving from supplying weapons to enabling Ukraine's domestic arms industry, a qualitative step that Russia has explicitly framed as direct involvement and that raises the risk of retaliation against British territory.

sections.heading: Colombia's New President Vows Mass Deportations of Venezuelan Migrants
sections.body:
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, sworn in three weeks ago and closely aligned with Donald Trump, has promised to deport thousands of migrants without residence permits, mainly Venezuelans, as part of a crime-reduction push, according to the Associated Press. He said he would order the national immigration service to conduct raids with police as early as this week, targeting first migrants 'committing crimes' and then those living without regular status.

'I will not accept any illegal immigrants, wherever they come from,' de la Espriella said in a video. Around 2.8 million Venezuelans were living in Colombia as of August, according to the United Nations, the largest Venezuelan diaspora, with about 2.3 million holding temporary residence permits granted under a 2021 scheme. The policy marks a major shift for Colombia, which had long worked to protect and regularize incoming Venezuelans.
sections.whyItMatters: Colombia hosts the world's largest Venezuelan diaspora, and a mass-deportation policy from a Trump-aligned president could reshape migration dynamics across South America and signal a broader regional turn away from the humanitarian approach that defined the past decade.

bottomLine: The day's defining development was Washington's formal removal of Syria from its terror list, a landmark that ends decades of isolation and opens the door to reconstruction financing, even as the US simultaneously escalated its economic war on Iran by sanctioning Tehran's trading partners under 'Operation Economic Outcast.' Pakistan reported significant progress in mediating the Iran conflict, the UK deepened its direct role in Ukraine by sharing missile blueprints, and Colombia's new president moved to deport Venezuelan migrants. The through-line is a Washington that is simultaneously reintegrating one former adversary, isolating another, and pushing allies and intermediaries to take sides in two overlapping wars.
